items.title: 'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes
items.summary: The BBC's Sarah Rainsford reports from the scene of a collapsed residential building in Ukraine's Kyiv region.
items.body:
'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes

'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes

At least three bodies have been recovered the site of a residential building that was hit by a Russian strike in the Kyiv region, Ukraine's State Emergency Services said.

A woman in her forties and a teenage boy have so far been identified as rescue workers continue to search the rubble for those who are still trapped.

Continued warnings of further drone threats near the site are hampering efforts, the service added, but some people were successfully evacuated earlier in the day.

"We are living a nightmare... only God knows when it will end," one woman told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford, who's reporting from Ukraine's Kyiv region.

items.title: Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy
items.summary: Laura Gallacher says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand Laura Gallacher, Russell Brand’s wife, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on…
items.body:
Laura Gallacher: ‘I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family.’ Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters

Laura Gallacher: ‘I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family.’ Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters

Russell Brand’s wife vows to abide by prison rules after video controversy

Laura Gallacher says in new video on YouTube she will continue Sunday Service series she started with Brand

Laura Gallacher, Russell Brand’s wife, has promised to “absolutely honour” rules set by the prison where her convicted sex offender husband is being held, in another YouTube video published on Sunday.

This week Andy Burnham called on Google to take down a video uploaded to Brand’s YouTube channel last Sunday that contained a statement from the disgraced comedian in prison, where he is serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults.

Gallacher began the latest episode of Sunday Service – described as a Christian series, which the couple started together six months ago – by telling viewers: “Last week’s episode drew considerable amount of attention and now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that.”

She went on to address scrutiny regarding her continuing to run her husband’s YouTube channel, amid a Ministry of Justice inquiry focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.

“I am choosing to continue Sunday Service because I really enjoy it,” Gallacher said. “It is also a place where I will continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media’s image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny.”

In the previous episode, the first published since Brand was jailed – after being convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November – Gallacher read out a message from him protesting that he was not guilty.

The video, titled “The Good Work Continues”, has remained on YouTube despite ministers repeatedly asking for it to be removed.

That video has now accumulated more than 1m views, becoming the best-performing video on Brand’s channel since 5 December last year, when he published a video conversation he had with the American conservative influencer Candace Owens. Many of his videos in the last year have drawn only between 50,000 and 100,000 views.

On Thursday night, Burnham said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down such content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. You know, why are we having to hear from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”

The prime minister faces pressure from the Conservatives to reduce the overall cost of working-age benefits. Photograph: Andriy Popov/Alamy

The prime minister faces pressure from the Conservatives to reduce the overall cost of working-age benefits. Photograph: Andriy Popov/Alamy

Pip review will call for overhaul rather than scrapping benefit for under-25s

Recommendations overseen by Stephen Timms would retain system for all ages, unlike last week’s Milburn review

A long-awaited review into the personal independence payment (Pip) system will this week recommend that it is overhauled – a week after another report called for it to be partly scrapped.

The final report into Pip by a committee co-led by Stephen Timms, the social security minister, is expected to be published as soon as Tuesday, presenting Andy Burnham with one of his most politically sensitive decisions yet as prime minister.

The review, shaped with the input of disability rights advocates, is understood to be very similar to a draft set of recommendations that emerged in September, which called for a series of changes, particularly to the system of assessment, to take better account of conditions that vary over time.

This would involve significant changes to Pip, which is intended to help disabled people meet the extra costs of disability. An interim report by Timms’ committee described the benefit as widely valued but “no longer fit for purpose”.

However, it would retain the system for all ages, while last week’s report by Alan Milburn into worklessness among young people called for it to be scrapped for adults under 25 and replaced by an “additional cost allowance”, part of a wider network of job-based help for this age group.

Government officials have pushed back on the idea of a clash, saying Milburn’s review was commissioned after the Timms process had begun, and that about 90% of the Pip caseload involved people over 25.

But with Timms’ recommendations understood to be quite broad, Burnham and his ministers will need to make a series of decisions about what comes next, on a deeply sensitive subject. Keir Starmer was forced to abandon planned changes in 2025 after a major rebellion by Labour MPs.

There was widespread shock among disability campaigners and charities at the Milburn report’s recommendations to scrap Pip and universal credit health benefit payments for under-25s as part of efforts to boost jobs and training for young people not in education, employment or training.

The review steering group is co-chaired by Timms and the disability rights advocates Clenton Farquharson and Sharon Brennan, with most of its 12 members having lived experience of disability or long-term health conditions.

There are reportedly worries among some members of the Timms review board over the scale of Milburn’s proposals on Pip, which would cut £3.6bn from spending on young people. “Some members are really concerned,” one source told the Guardian.

The report will include short-term overhauls, within the current spending round, and longer-term ones. Many of the specifics for the latter would need to be decided by ministers before they legislate next year.

The prime minister faces pressure from the Conservatives to reduce the overall cost of working-age benefits. Burnham has said this is his plan but has pushed back against the idea of what he called “crude cuts”, saying these often just created costs elsewhere.

The Timms review, framed by ministers as a groundbreaking “co-produced” policy initiative, was seen as an attempt to restore trust among disabled people after the collapse of the Pip plans under Starmer, which were based around £5bn in cuts.

The interim report in July and further emerging findings in September confirmed a consensus view that Pip was unfit for purpose, and that a major overhaul was needed to make the benefit fair, humane and efficient. It raised the prospect that some claimants could in future receive “in kind” awards such as services, aids or training alongside basic cash awards.

But it underlined that cash payments were “the foundation” of a future reformed disability benefit, that it would be non-means tested and that any “reformed benefit will be designed with disabled people and those with long-term health conditions, and tested to make sure it works before it is rolled out”. There was no mention of scrapping Pip for under-25s, or any other age groups.

Until recently, most disability charities had been optimistic that the Timms review – the remit of which did not include the costs of Pip or potential cuts in spending – would lead to much-needed changes and improve the lives of the 4 million adults who claim it.

But the timing and scope of the Milburn review, which has been conspicuously welcomed by ministers, has dented that confidence.

items.title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
items.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone strike on Saturday. Kyiv has yet to comment.
items.body:
Image source, Finnish Border Guard

Image caption,

The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 43 minutes ago

A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

items.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
items.summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
items.body:
Image source, Planet Labs PBC

Image caption,

Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire early on Sunday morning

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 4 minutes ago

An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.

It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS said the country was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Seperately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

Smoke rises from a fire after an explosion on Merkury, a Russian warship docked at Benghazi port, Libya. Photograph: 2026 Planet Labs PBC/Reuters

Blast on Russian ship in Benghazi a suspected drone attack, say Libyan authorities

No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia

An explosion on a Russian ship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya’s eastern-based government has said.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the suspected strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

“Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred onboard a Russian ship docked in the port,” said the administration backed by the military commander Khalifa Haftar. “It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones.”

Authorities in divided Libya’s east said the vessel had stopped at Benghazi port to refuel and ⁠resupply on its way back to Russia, ​under maritime cooperation agreements between ‌the two ‌countries.

Two medical sources said no deaths had been ‌reported from the blast, but there were injuries. The number and nationalities of those injured are not yet known.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.

An explosion on the ship in Benghazi, where it had been refuelling on its way back to Russia. Photograph: X.com

The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.

“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the five-year war.

But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians in another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Initial reports and footage suggest the ship was struck from above, potentially by a drone, launched no more than a few kilometres away from the target in port.

Russia is close to the Benghazi authorities that control eastern Libya. It uses the port to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean, which has a growing importance after it lost bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

Emergency services are working to extinguish a fire onboard the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which was struck in the Baltic Sea. Photograph: Finnish Border Guard/Reuters

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.

On Sunday visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

Pictures ​and video released earlier by the Finnish coastguard showed several ‌vessels spraying the Sparta II with ‌water cannons during the night in an attempt to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.

“Smoke is still coming from the vessel, and ​there is clearly still heat onboard,” said Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, a sea safety officer and commander of the maritime sub-centre Helsinki for the Finnish border guard, at a press conference on Sunday.

Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

The Cop31 president, Murat Kurum, at the closing plenary session. Photograph: Abdullah Guclu/Anadolu/Getty Images

The Cop31 president, Murat Kurum, at the closing plenary session. Photograph: Abdullah Guclu/Anadolu/Getty Images

Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected

EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ after two weeks of fierce negotiations

Cop31 live blog: longest climate summit ever faces collapse

The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that campaigners have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.

But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and many developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be the “cover decision”, or main outcome, of the Cop.

In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Darragh O’Brien (centre) and Wopke Hoekstra, the EU climate commissioner, speak outside a plenary session at Cop31 on Sunday. Photograph: Khalil Hamra/AP

His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.

“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.

Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations.

after newsletter promotion

Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.

For many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis. Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, while African ministers made a dramatic intervention on Friday saying: “We did not come here to beg.”

Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, summed up the view of many on Friday when he said: “The Cop presidents want to tell us this has been a great Cop. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst Cop ever.”

On Sunday, he added: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create.... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.

“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”

While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.

“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

items.summary: Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking th…
items.body:
Theresa May might not like the idea of revisiting Brexit but did not even try to argue that it had been a success. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock

Theresa May might not like the idea of revisiting Brexit but did not even try to argue that it had been a success. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock

Analysis

Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place

Peter Walker

Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere

Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea.

This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place.

For Tory MPs and activists with a full set of Brexit campaign medals, this risks being especially triggering. May’s repeated attempts to cobble together a departure deal that could unite her party involved repeated humiliations, among them the heaviest ever parliamentary defeat for a British PM, when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by a majority of 230.

With the afterglow of Boris Johnson’s “get Brexit done” 2019 election triumph now seven years and four prime ministers ago, under Kemi Badenoch the party has opted to do less of the, in David Cameron’s resonant phrase, “banging on about Europe” and instead focus on policy areas such as the economy, social security and defence.

The reasons for this caution are obvious. To begin with, even more ardent Tory Brexiters struggle to articulate any tangible benefits to the UK in the decade since the referendum, beyond slightly niche constitutional points about self-determination.

In her BBC interview, May, who comments sparingly on live political subjects despite being an active Tory peer, did not even try to argue that Brexit had been a success, instead saying it was impossible to know, given events such as Covid and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and then adding: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union.”

Many voters are much clearer about what they think. Polling suggests that a clear majority of Britons view Brexit as both a failure and a mistake in the first place, with similar support for rejoining the EU, although this depends in part on the pre-conditions for doing so.

This is a product of both lived experience and what pollsters delicately call “demographic churn” – that is, the death of many of the disproportionately older Britons who voted leave and their replacement on the electoral rolls by younger people with more positive views about the EU.

after newsletter promotion

Closer EU ties will give UK say on Brussels decisions, says Ed Miliband

Read more

A new constituency-level poll on Brexit sentiment found that hundreds of previously leave-backing areas, including Burnham’s Makerfield seat, now support rejoining.

Of the 632 Commons seats in England, Scotland and Wales, it found that voters in 512 would rejoin the EU, with 47 too close to call. Just 73 areas – slightly over 11% of the total – still want to stay out.

For the Conservatives, the battle has not ended. Badenoch will lambast the PM when he sets out his new EU deal in parliament on Monday. Her deputy, Alex Burghart, has already promised that a future Tory government would unpick it.

But make no mistake, Europe is no longer the Conservatives’ defining political thread, and division, as it was for several decades. May might, understandably, be unable to move on from the issue that made her PM and then destroyed her career. But her party, like the country, has no choice.

A towering Bigfoot statue stands in Cataloochee, North Carolina, in the Smoky Mountains valley. Photograph: Franck Fotos/Alamy

A towering Bigfoot statue stands in Cataloochee, North Carolina, in the Smoky Mountains valley. Photograph: Franck Fotos/Alamy

US releases files on suspected Bigfoot sightings in Montana and Oregon

Forest Service releases files months after residents in rural Ontario reported encounters with massive figures

Bigfoot has quietly appeared again.

Well, not Sasquatch directly, but new files about the cryptid.

In a public archive, the US Forest Service recently added reports concerning suspected encounters with Bigfoot – or its remnants in Montana and Oregon.

A newly released 1982 report showed how a wildlife biologist investigated peculiar tracks in north-east Oregon.

The additional documents also included a 2003 Montana newspaper story about a reported sighting of Bigfoot tracks and a testimonial about the history of a creek area in Montana where people spotted what they thought was “a very large bear, except bears don’t walk on their hind legs only for short distances”.

The recent release of the files by the US Forest Service comes months after residents in rural Ontario, Canada, reported encounters with massive figures that matched the description of Bigfoot.

Collectively, they add to a long history of suspected sightings of Bigfoot or markings from the bipedal ape whose existence has not been confirmed by science. The Bigfoot Mapping Project contains more than 16,000 reports on the cryptid, a term referring to an animal or creature whose existence has not been proven.

Carleton University philosophy professor Josh Redstone previously told the Guardian that Bigfoot is a prime example of how fascinating the unverified can be for humans.

“For people who believe in Sasquatch, there’s an excitement around the possibility of discovering something new,” Redstone said.

In the 1982 report, the biologist, Rodney Johnson, investigated tracks at three locations in the Umatilla National Forest in north-east Oregon. To determine their origin, Johnson – or a fellow investigator – made plaster casts of two of the tracks.

Johnson gave eight reasons why he did not think the tracks belonged to Sasquatch, including:

• “The stride of the tracks did not change with slope.”

• “The tracks at both sites were not to the ‘bottom’ of the mud.

• “The small toes lack a definite ‘pad’ at the tips as would be expected.”

Still, Johnson did not entirely dismiss the Bigfoot theory.

“If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail,” Johnson wrote. “The ‘print’ marks on the foot would have to be very hard to duplicate. They appear very natural. I would almost suspect a cast made of an actual foot would have had to be used to make the ‘fake’ feet. If this were the case though, the other creases in the foot should have shown.”

In a subsequent report from the forest service, the investigator stated that the tracks “were a very clever attempt to perpetrate a hoax”.

“Trusting that this memo will suffice to close this ‘Bigfoot’ case,” the report stated.

That case might have been closed – but there were others.

In the 1980 testimonial, which reads like a novel, Leo Kinney in Montana wrote: “Now to tell some of the things that made history.”

He and three others entered the woods to retrieve an elk carcass, he wrote. But he said they instead spotted “another type creature that walked on its hind legs that altho [sic] there wasn’t actual sightings, tracks, a strong odor and a gruntling sound were observed”.

After determining that the creature had supposedly picked up the elk and dragged it, “we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was and tho [sic] we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.”

The journalist who produced the 2003 Clark Fork Valley Press story wrote that a group in Montana found hundreds of “strange footprints”.

“I didn’t believe it until I saw the tracks,” one woman said.

Residents in rural Ontario in June reported seeing two creatures scavenging through garbage.

“One big, one not so big,” an account stated. “The cinnamon was prominent on the smaller one.”

All who believe they have spotted a trace of Bigfoot submit a report to the Bigfoot Mapping Project.

After determining that the creature had supposedly picked up the elk and dragged it, “we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was and tho [sic] we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.”
The journalist who produced the 2003 Clark Fork Valley Press story wrote that a group in Montana found hundreds of “strange footprints”.
“I didn’t believe it until I saw the tracks,” one woman said.
Residents in rural Ontario in June reported seeing two creatures scavenging through garbage.
“One big, one not so big,” an account stated. “The cinnamon was prominent on the smaller one.”

items.summary: Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama, raising fears over cost to public purse The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purs…
items.body:

Road Town, on Tortola island, the capital of the British Virgin Islands, a major offshore financial centre known for its low taxes and corporate secrecy. Photograph: Todd VanSickle/AP

UK taxpayer funds held in offshore tax havens top £1tn, latest HMRC data shows

Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama raising fears over cost to public purse

The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures.

The list of tax havens represented in the HMRC data was based on one originally put together by academics from the EU Tax Observatory, and includes jurisdictions such as Hong Kong, the Isle of Jersey, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Panama.

‘A mockery’: how offshore tax havens are thwarting the UK’s transparency push

Read more

While much of the money in the offshore accounts will have been correctly declared to the UK’s tax authority, large sums are still proving hard to track down and claw back.

HMRC managed to secure an average of £125m in previously unpaid tax, interest on penalties, from offshore accounts – including those held in tax havens – each year, according to the data provided to TaxWatch.

That is thanks to information shared through agreements such as the common reporting standard (CRS), which commits countries to exchange information about foreigners’ bank accounts, as part of efforts to crack down on tax evasion and fraud.

However, HMRC previously estimated that £200m to £700m was going unpaid across all offshore accounts on average each year, according to a 2018 snapshot it provided.

And TaxWatch said about a fifth of offshore accounts owned by UK taxpayers were declared through the CRS system without a unique taxpayer identifier, which are meant to be gathered by the banks or financial firms that hold the accounts. That makes it difficult for HMRC to match undeclared accounts with individual taxpayers.

That has raised concerns about how much potential UK tax revenue may be disappearing via accounts held in tax havens, such as the British Virgin Islands and Bermuda, which are known for their low taxes and corporate secrecy.

HMRC announced plans to clamp down on wealthy taxpayers recently, including those who may be storing assets overseas.

That has involved assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires, to help tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they should. HMRC estimates it could end up raising at least £500m towards a larger commitment to secure £10bn of additional tax revenues by 2030.

HMRC was grilled in July last year by MPs on the parliamentary public accounts committee over its lack of understanding of tax compliance by about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.

after newsletter promotion

Mike Lewis, the director of TaxWatch, said: “Last month’s budget brought the welcome announcement of a new HMRC plan to increase wealthy and offshore tax compliance. These new figures show that plan will require more resources, expertise and time.

“Much less unpaid tax is being recovered from offshore accounts than HMRC’s estimate of tax evasion in such accounts – an estimate which only covers accounts automatically notified to HMRC, and which UK taxpayers hold in their own names.

“That’s the lowest-hanging fruit. Most tax evasion happens behind much more complex structures.”

TaxWatch said HMRC had repeatedly postponed publishing estimates of all the tax going unpaid on offshore income and gains, leaving the public and government unable to properly benchmark the tax authority’s effectiveness in tackling offshore tax evasion and non-compliance.

An HMRC spokesperson said: “We’ve led the way in increasing global tax transparency, helping us tackle offshore tax risks and ensure everyone pays the right amount under UK law.

“We’ve already strengthened our approach by bringing together specialist expertise to take on the most complex offshore risks, and we’re deploying an additional 400 people to tackle wealthy offshore non-compliance by 2030.”

items.summary: Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposi…
items.body:
Israeli settlers torched cars belonging to Palestinians in the West Bank village of Kafr Malik on Saturday night. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA

Israeli settlers torched cars belonging to Palestinians in the West Bank village of Kafr Malik on Saturday night. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA

Netanyahu rival condemns settler arson attacks on Palestinian villages in West Bank

Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes

Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.

Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.

Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.

A Palestinian man inspects the damage after the attack. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA

An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.

“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”

Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”

Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.

In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.

The village of Deir Abu Mashal, near Ramallah, was also targeted. Photograph: Issam Rimawi/Anadolu/Getty Images

Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.

Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.

“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”

Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.

Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.

A burnt-out car in Kafr Malik. The Israeli politician Yair Lapid said Benjamin Netanyahu’s government had encouraged the attacks. Photograph: Issam Rimawi/Anadolu/Getty Images

Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

Reuters contributed to this report

items.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
items.summary: At least three people were killed and many more feared dead after a fire at a confectionary factory.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

At least three people have been killed and 36 were still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 1630 local time (0930 GMT) but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.

"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.

The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.

On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

items.summary: One serial sweary offender, Jacqui Lambie, says it wouldn’t be an Australian parliament ‘without a few swear words thrown in’ Want to get more charts in your inbox every fortnight? items.body:
Senator Jacqui Lambie is responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament, at a rate of 406 swear words per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images

Senator Jacqui Lambie is responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament, at a rate of 406 swear words per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images

Potty-mouthed MPs ranked as Australian parliament sets new swearing record

One serial sweary offender, Jacqui Lambie, says it wouldn’t be an Australian parliament ‘without a few swear words thrown in’

• Want to get more charts in your inbox every fortnight? Sign up for The Crunch here

When Liberal MP Garth Hamilton stormed out of parliament in June, slamming his hands on his desk and calling out “fucking bullshit” the speaker of the house, Milton Dick, called it “a new low” in federal politics.

Dick may have been on to something.

New analysis from Guardian Australia has found profanity and foul language has risen significantly in Australia’s parliament over the past 20 years, with some of today’s most prominent politicians among the chief culprits for swearing.

Before the year is even out, 2026 is the worst year on record for the use of swear words and language deemed “unparliamentary”. That number has risen by 78% since 2006.

Analysis of Hansard debate and procedure records has found that per million words spoken in parliament this year, approximately 37 have been profane – ranging from milder (“bloody”, “damn” and “crap”) to language considered strong, or even extreme.

Line chart showing swear words per million words spoken in the Australian parliament from 2006 to 2026. The rate fluctuates but trends upwards, rising from about 16 in 2006 to a peak of 37 in 2026, with a low of around 12 in 2009. A dotted trend line highlights the overall increase.

While entitled to “parle hard”, language deemed unparliamentary by the speaker or Senate president is required to be withdrawn, or else MPs face ejection from the chamber.

So why bother?

Beyond the impact of pushing against regulation and etiquette, there is something to be said for the currency that outbursts gain when clipped and shared online – recently demonstrated by Greens senator Peter Whish-Wilson, who called for the country to “wake the fuck up” to One Nation’s use of social media algorithms in June.

But despite the politicians reaching for profanities at a record rate, Dick – the Labor MP who has been speaker of the house since 2022 – said he felt the tone and tenor of debate in parliament has gotten better in his time in the chair.

“Debate is fierce and strong, and apart from a few incidents, it has improved,” he said.

“Maybe it hasn’t appeared so because of the volume [of swearing], but when you analyse the words used … there are outbreaks of course, but I believe in everyone showing respect.”

And to be fair, most of parliament’s most swear-y politicians are in the Senate, not the house.

An oral tradition

Described as “the great Australian adjective” in 1894 by The Bulletin magazine, “bloody” appears to have suffered no fall from grace in the subsequent years, serving as the most commonly used swear word in parliament. Along with “damn”, “crap” and “bugger”, mild curses constitute 92% of all recorded bad language, with more severe terms such as “prick”, “shit” and “piss” used more sparingly.

Excluded from this figure are rare cases of colourful and creative terms that have been called for withdrawal. Harnessing the speaker’s unilateral power to flag unacceptable language, terms such as “bin chickens – used by Julian Hill, the MP for Bruce, in 2022 to describe the opposition in the house – have been ruled as unparliamentary.

Swearing and swearing allegiance

Much of this potty-talk comes from the Senate, which since 2006 has seen a 177% increase in the use of bad language. Among active parliamentary participants (those who have spoken at least 100,000 words in this period), Bill Heffernan was the lead offender. Despite speaking just 141,000 words between 2006 and 2016, the former Liberal senator had an expletive use-rate of 877 per million words spoken, 43 times the rate of all other parliamentarians.

Stacked bar chart showing swear words per million words spoken in the Australian parliament, 2006–2026. Bill Heffernan leads with 877.2, followed by Jacqui Lambie (406.3), Derryn Hinch (398.4), Glenn Sterle (294.3), Russell Matheson (206.9), David Shoebridge (179.5), Pauline Hanson (169.5), Jordon Steele-John (167.9) and Steph Hodgins-May (161.6). Mild swear words make up most of each total, with smaller contributions from strong and extreme language. Only politicians who spoke more than 100,000 words are included.

Jacqui Lambie is the second-most sweary politician, responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament at a rate of 406 per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. But, like most of the politicians on this list, Lambie’s swearing is overwhelmingly mild – mostly words like “crap” or “bloody”.

“I try really hard not to swear, especially in the Senate chamber. It upsets my mum, she doesn’t even like me saying ‘bloody’,” Lambie said when we came to her with the statistics.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

“It’s important to be respectful. But I am a straight shooter and sometimes things are just crap – and it’s hard not to say so. I don’t think it would be an Australian parliament without a few swear words thrown in.”

Not all occurrences of swearing in parliamentary records are “own-use”, or rather, swearing with intent. Quotes, such as reading out abuse a politician has received, or a quote from a document, account for some of it.

However, when excluding these cases our analysis shows that own-use swearing in parliament has nearly tripled over the last 20 years, from 6.4 per million words in 2006-9, to 18.9 in 2022-5.

Line chart showing the three-year rolling rate of politicians’ own-use swearing per million words spoken in the Australian parliament, by party, from 2008 to 2026. One Nation peaks at about 175 in 2024 before falling to 110 in 2026. The Greens rise unevenly, reaching nearly 100 in 2026. Independents peak at about 80 in 2017 before declining sharply. Labor and Liberal rates remain below 15 throughout, while the Nationals reach about 24 in 2026.

Broken down by party, One Nation are the worst offenders, swearing for the sake of it at 7.4 times the rate of Labor – perhaps unsurprising, given that the party leader, Pauline Hanson, ranks fourth among discursively active politicians for use of foul language.

Dick said he had strived to improve the tone of discussion in parliament, believing that greater diversity in politics and in the chamber – with more women, more First Nations MPs and people from multicultural backgrounds – had also changed dynamics of debate.

Asked about recent heated moments in parliament, he said he recalled only two major moments in the lower house in recent years Hamilton’s June storm-out and fellow Liberal MP Dan Tehan’s demand to “cut the crap” in August.

“I want to ensure among our people and our democracy, that we fight hard to disagree more civilly … But I’m a big believer in upholding traditions and standards. When things get a bit heated, I’ll take firm action,” Dick said.

Notes on the analysis

Politicians’ speeches from both Houses of Parliament were analysed for the years 2006 to 2026. For each speech, the number of swearwords were counted using the these categories:

• Mild: bloody, damn, crap, bugger, bastard, bulldust, arse, mongrel, boofhead, bollocks

blocks.text: When Liberal MP Garth Hamilton stormed out of parliament in June, slamming his hands on his desk and calling out “fucking bullshit” the speaker of the house, Milton Dick, called it “a new low” in federal politics.
Dick may have been on to something.

New analysis from Guardian Australia has found profanity and foul language has risen significantly in Australia’s parliament over the past 20 years, with some of today’s most prominent politicians among the chief culprits for swearing.
Before the year is even out, 2026 is the worst year on record for the use of swear words and language deemed “unparliamentary”. That number has risen by 78% since 2006.

Analysis of Hansard debate and procedure records has found that per million words spoken in parliament this year, approximately 37 have been profane – ranging from milder (“bloody”, “damn” and “crap”) to language considered strong, or even extreme.

Line chart showing swear words per million words spoken in the Australian parliament from 2006 to 2026. The rate fluctuates but trends upwards, rising from about 16 in 2006 to a peak of 37 in 2026, with a low of around 12 in 2009. A dotted trend line highlights the overall increase.
While entitled to “parle hard”, language deemed unparliamentary by the speaker or Senate president is required to be withdrawn, or else MPs face ejection from the chamber.
So why bother?

Beyond the impact of pushing against regulation and etiquette, there is something to be said for the currency that outbursts gain when clipped and shared online – recently demonstrated by Greens senator Peter Whish-Wilson, who called for the country to “wake the fuck up” to One Nation’s use of social media algorithms in June.

But despite the politicians reaching for profanities at a record rate, Dick – the Labor MP who has been speaker of the house since 2022 – said he felt the tone and tenor of debate in parliament has gotten better in his time in the chair.
“Debate is fierce and strong, and apart from a few incidents, it has improved,” he said.
“Maybe it hasn’t appeared so because of the volume [of swearing], but when you analyse the words used … there are outbreaks of course, but I believe in everyone showing respect.”
And to be fair, most of parliament’s most swear-y politicians are in the Senate, not the house.
An oral tradition

Described as “the great Australian adjective” in 1894 by The Bulletin magazine, “bloody” appears to have suffered no fall from grace in the subsequent years, serving as the most commonly used swear word in parliament. Along with “damn”, “crap” and “bugger”, mild curses constitute 92% of all recorded bad language, with more severe terms such as “prick”, “shit” and “piss” used more sparingly.

Excluded from this figure are rare cases of colourful and creative terms that have been called for withdrawal. Harnessing the speaker’s unilateral power to flag unacceptable language, terms such as “bin chickens – used by Julian Hill, the MP for Bruce, in 2022 to describe the opposition in the house – have been ruled as unparliamentary.
Swearing and swearing allegiance

Much of this potty-talk comes from the Senate, which since 2006 has seen a 177% increase in the use of bad language. Among active parliamentary participants (those who have spoken at least 100,000 words in this period), Bill Heffernan was the lead offender. Despite speaking just 141,000 words between 2006 and 2016, the former Liberal senator had an expletive use-rate of 877 per million words spoken, 43 times the rate of all other parliamentarians.

Stacked bar chart showing swear words per million words spoken in the Australian parliament, 2006–2026. Bill Heffernan leads with 877.2, followed by Jacqui Lambie (406.3), Derryn Hinch (398.4), Glenn Sterle (294.3), Russell Matheson (206.9), David Shoebridge (179.5), Pauline Hanson (169.5), Jordon Steele-John (167.9) and Steph Hodgins-May (161.6). Mild swear words make up most of each total, with smaller contributions from strong and extreme language. Only politicians who spoke more than 100,000 words are included.

Jacqui Lambie is the second-most sweary politician, responsible for 6% of total swearing in parliament at a rate of 406 per million words spoken – more than 19 times the average. But, like most of the politicians on this list, Lambie’s swearing is overwhelmingly mild – mostly words like “crap” or “bloody”.
“I try really hard not to swear, especially in the Senate chamber. It upsets my mum, she doesn’t even like me saying ‘bloody’,” Lambie said when we came to her with the statistics.

“It’s important to be respectful. But I am a straight shooter and sometimes things are just crap – and it’s hard not to say so. I don’t think it would be an Australian parliament without a few swear words thrown in.”

Not all occurrences of swearing in parliamentary records are “own-use”, or rather, swearing with intent. Quotes, such as reading out abuse a politician has received, or a quote from a document, account for some of it.
However, when excluding these cases our analysis shows that own-use swearing in parliament has nearly tripled over the last 20 years, from 6.4 per million words in 2006-9, to 18.9 in 2022-5.

Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam th…
items.body:
Lewis Pugh during his three-day, 9.3-mile swim through the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AP

Lewis Pugh during his three-day, 9.3-mile swim through the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AP

Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war

UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues

A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.

Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.

An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”

A vessel on fire in the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AFP/Getty Images

The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems

Read more

Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.

He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”

The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.

Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.

Pugh, 56, is a UN patron of the oceans. Photograph: Lewis Pugh Foundation/AFP/Getty Images

The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.

Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

NFL’s Jaylen Harrell reportedly assaulted driver before crash that left player seriously injured

• Incident occurred in Tampa on Friday morning

• Crash leaves linebacker with serious injuries

Tampa police are investigating whether Tennessee Titans linebacker Jaylen Harrell assaulted a rideshare driver before a crash that left the NFL player in hospital.

The Tampa ⁠Police Department, in ⁠a preliminary report, said Harrell was in the back seat of the car around 8.45am on Friday in the backseat when “he reportedly assaulted the driver while ⁠the vehicle was in motion.” The driver then swerved, struck another car and collided ⁠with a utility pole, per the police report.

Harrell was thrown from the backseat, hit the windshield ‌and lost consciousness, according to ‌the police report. Harrell remains in hospital with serious injuries, while the rideshare ‌driver, a man in his 30s, sustained “minor injuries” and was treated at the scene, according to police. The driver of the other vehicle, a woman in her 50s, was not injured, the police said.

The Titans issued a statement on Saturday ‌morning but did not disclose Harrell’s condition or the injuries he suffered, nor did they mention the assault accusation. The 24-year-old has not played this season after tearing an ACL in the preseason.

“We have been in constant communication with Jaylen’s family and are still working to gather more information,” the team said ⁠in the statement. “At this time, Jaylen remains in the hospital and continues to receive care. We ask that Jaylen and his family’s privacy be respected at this time. We will provide an ‌update when appropriate.”

The accident occurred in Tampa, Harrell’s hometown.

Harrell played college football at Michigan before the Titans picked him in the seventh round of the 2024 draft. He played in every game in his first two seasons and recorded 4.5 sacks. His father, James, played eight seasons in the NFL before becoming a successful high school coach.

items.title: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams
items.summary: Choi Kyo-jin says he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams following last-minute scramble to tighten measures South Korea’s education minister has resigned after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to key university entrance exams last week. The country has been g…
items.body:
Students at a high school in Seoul during South Korea's annual suneung exams, which this year were upended by an AI cheating scandal. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Students at a high school in Seoul during South Korea's annual suneung exams, which this year were upended by an AI cheating scandal. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

South Korea education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams

Choi Kyo-jin said he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams, which this year had phones banned and checks for cameras hidden in clothing

South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.

The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.

The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the entrance exams last week, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.

But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.

South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal

Read more

The annual eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

“The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X.

“Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.

President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation, the presidential office said.

A student turns in her tablet and smartphone at a high school in Seoul ahead of the suneung exams. Photograph: Jintak Han/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old Choi replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response quickly drew public backlash.

Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, where a vice minister instead announced the preventive measures.

South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.

In the aftermath of the cheating scandal earlier this month, the government announced that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.

The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

Officials said 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.

items.body:
Iain Barbour (left) and his brother Stuart from Jamieson Brothers, a Scottish seed potato supplier. Photograph: Jamieson Brothers

Iain Barbour (left) and his brother Stuart from Jamieson Brothers, a Scottish seed potato supplier. Photograph: Jamieson Brothers

UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’

Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long

British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.

The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.

However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.

“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.

Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.

The exclusion particularly hit the Scottish industry, whose farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world, as well as growers in northern England. Scottish seed potato farmers previously accounted for three-quarters of UK production and the sector was worth about £112m a year.

Ireland and the EU represented a fifth of Jamieson Brothers’ trade before Brexit. The company particularly suffered from the loss of the Irish business, given it grew many varieties that were popular on plates in the north and south of Ireland.

Scottish potato farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world before Brexit. Photograph: Skully/Alamy

While the company adapted its business to start packing work that would have previously been carried out in the EU, Barbour estimates this change cost about £500,000.

“We evolved, we worked with more partners and that’s what kept the business going,” Barbour said.

Barbour is looking forward to supplying his Irish customers once againHowever, he said it would take at least three years until he could revive varieties that were no longer being grown and were instead stored in a seed bank.

“A lot of Scottish farmers stopped producing varieties that were popular in Ireland as they weren’t desired in England. Varieties that had been going about 100 years were killed off in a couple of years,” he said. “So we’ll have to look at bringing them back.”

The planned implementation of the food deal in March 2028 would also be “a couple of months late for the trade”, given most sales happen at the start of the year and the crops needs to be grown in advance.

Barbour anticipates most growers will be wary and will only fully resume trading in 2029. “People are obviously going to be a little bit hesitant to grow anything until it’s 100% official,” he said.

Devon’s Offshore Shellfish has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite post-Brexit red tape. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

British exporters of live bivalve molluscs – the collective term for shellfish including mussels, oysters, clams, cockles and scallops – hope the deal will give the sector a shot in the arm.

The industry is small and specialised. It was valued at less than £12m a year before Brexit, but it is crucial for some coastal communities.

Offshore Shellfish, a family-run business produces rope-grown mussels in the waters of Lyme Bay, Devon, has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite the administrative burden and occasional blocks by French customs.

The company exports the vast majority of the blue mussels it produces. It sends to the Netherlands for processing, before most end up in restaurants or on supermarket shelves in Belgium, where they are prized as a key ingredient in moules-frites, one of the country’s national dishes.

Offshore Shellfish’s Sarah Holmyard says the deal’s provisions are ‘a huge win for us’. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

Sarah Holmyard, the commercial director of Offshore Shellfish, said the most important detail was an assurance that the deal would allow live bivalve molluscs to be exported even if they did not come from waters with the highest quality rating.

Offshore Shellfish’s farms are in waters which are considered “class A” for most of the year, but before the new SPS deal, any change in water quality to “class B” could have temporarily halted exports.

“That’s a huge win for us because we’ve been pushing and pushing and pushing for that,” Holmyard said.

However, the deal will come too late for those UK shellfish producers that have closed down since Brexit. Three out of four mussel fishing companies in the Menai strait, the channel that separates the north Wales mainland from the island of Anglesey, stopped trading after exports became too difficult.

The promised end of physical border checks on dairy, fish and meat products was welcomed by Rich Clothier, the managing director of Wyke Farms. The Somerset-based cheese and butter maker exports about a quarter of its cheddar to the EU, particularly France, Germany and Spain.

Rich Clothier, the managing director of cheesemaker Wyke Farms, says the deal ‘will save a huge amount of cost and product waste’. Photograph: Josh Campbell

Dairy exports to the EU have been less contentious since Brexit than seed potatoes or mussels, but not without challenges. The removal of veterinary checks is viewed as a significant benefit by Clothier.

“It’s a very bureaucratic process to get everything signed off, in what is not a very modern sort of system,” he said. “The agreement will save a huge amount of cost and product waste as well, because these are perishable.

“Any reduction in friction saves cost, it makes business more efficient. But it is really frustrating that it’s going to take so long [to be implemented] because, to be honest, we’re all pretty aligned anyway.”

items.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
items.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
items.body:
Figure caption,

How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam

ByJaroslav Lukiv

South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.

He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.

The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.

Image source, EPA/Shutterstock

Image caption,

South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.

"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.

The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.

Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.

His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.

This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.

This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.
